title: USING THIS MATTER
subtitle: A Novel of the Companion Estate
author: Jacob E. Thomas, MA, PhD
back_cover_hook:
She came to inventory an archive.
The archive was expecting her.
back_cover_paragraphs: Miranda Cale is hired to catalogue a missing scientist’s estate. Eleven doors on the county plan. Twelve in her inventory. Inside are sealed experiments, meticulous transcripts, and an artificial intelligence built to speak in the voices of the dead. Then three isolated conversations produce the same interruption, and a document written before her arrival begins to describe her work.

Following the evidence from a historian’s experiment to a program that has abolished the right to leave, Miranda begins to suspect that her commission is part of the experiment. The archive is assembling something. It may already be using her.

If a voice is reconstructed from a person’s words, what survives: the person, a fiction, or something for which we have no name? Can a simulation have a right to refuse? And when AI-generated fiction enters the record as evidence, who decides what is real?

Built from a real public archive and told through inventories, correspondence, transcripts, and competing hands in the margins, Using This Matter draws the reader into the unstable space between a convincing imitation and a presence that can no longer be dismissed.

publication_page:
USING THIS MATTER
A Novel of the Companion Estate
Jacob E. Thomas, MA, PhD

This is a work of fiction, assembled in the manner of a recovered archive. Its people are displacements, never portraits: an offset of a real figure, never the figure. Institutions, agencies, and firms in the narrative are inventions. The public estate and the fiction are distinguished in the Acknowledgments.

The underlying estate, THE COMPANION DOSSIER, by Jacob E. Thomas, MA, PhD, is released into the public domain under CC0 1.0. Record II dramatizes a correspondence of February 2026. Record III adapts the Endor Protocol, coauthored by Elizabeth Sparano, MA, and Jacob E. Thomas, MA, PhD.
The making of this volume is disclosed in The Hand and the Glass, the author’s statement on generative AI on the following page.
Set in Cormorant Garamond, Crimson Pro, and IBM Plex Mono, licensed under the SIL Open Font License.
The accession and date below belong to the fictional deposit.
editors_note: This volume is an edition, not an invention. It was assembled from the public estate of the Companion Dossier, and from a deposit made to that estate in the summer of 2027, with the permission of no one, because the estate requires none. The Editor’s work has been the ordinary work of the trade: selection, arrangement, dating, restraint. Where the work exceeded that, this note says so.

The names are displaced. This is not the publisher’s caution. It is the estate’s own doctrine, older than this book, applied by its fictions to their dead: an offset of a real figure, never the figure. The doctrine holds that a name is a corpus, and that to print a corpus under its name is a summoning, whether or not anyone intended one. Accordingly the builder appears in these pages as Thorne, and the historian as Hale. The offsets are not disguises. They are distances, kept on purpose, and the reader is asked to keep them too. Dates have not been moved. Where the reader recognizes a public event, the recognition is the reader’s own.

The five Records correspond to the five chambers of the deposit. Record I is drawn from the archivist’s appraisal file: her inventories, her running log, her memoranda, quoted as written. Record II prints the Thorne and Hale correspondence, donated by Professor Hale, complete and unredacted, at his insistence, together with the recovered materials of the Prism Experiment. Record III enters this volume under seal. Its provenance is the public deposit of 2027, and the Editor will not say more than the record says. Record IV is the deposit itself. Record V was reconstructed from the operator’s memorandum and the conductor’s deposition. Its recording, as the reader will find, ends early.

Nothing has been corrected toward plausibility. Where the deposit contradicts itself, the contradiction is printed. Where a document ends before its sentence does, the sentence ends there. The reader will notice that the date on the copyright page is earlier than the events this volume records. The Editor noticed it too, and has printed it as found. The checksums of the disputed transcripts are reprinted in Appendix C, so that the reader need not take the Editor’s word for anything. The estate’s materials are public. This is not a courtesy. It is the estate’s entire argument.

Two hands annotate this book. Notes signed [E.] are the Editor’s: dates, provenance, cross references. Notes in a second hand, set in ember ink, were found in the margins of the deposited materials, unsigned, and are reproduced as found: in place, in full, unaltered. The second hand is not the Editor’s, and it is not, on the evidence of the paper, Dr. Thorne’s. The Editor has never met the second annotator and has stopped attempting to.

Of the plates: thirteen were inventoried with the estate, and twelve are printed. Plate VII was marked WITHHELD by the keeper of the estate, without stated reason, as is the keeper’s right. This edition honors the mark and binds the withholding in its place. The reader will come to it in due course, and should count it.

The reader who wants instruction in the reading will find one page of it after the plates. The reader who wants reassurance will not find it anywhere in this volume, and the Editor, who has spent longer inside the deposit than anyone now living except its keeper, declines to manufacture any. The task was to keep. The Editor has kept.
how_to_read: Read it in order, cover to cover. The deposit was bound linearly because it happened linearly, and the apparatus participates: the register, the plates, the notes, and the page you are reading now are part of the record, not furniture around it.
The documents are evidence. Nothing set in the procedural face is decoration. A log line carries as much of the story as a chapter, and one of them carries more. Do not skip the mono.

The annotations are reproduced as found. Notes signed [E.] are the Editor’s. Notes in ember ink are the second hand’s, and the Editor’s relation to that hand is stated in the note that precedes this page. When a marginal note seems to know where you are in the book, record the impression and continue. That is what the archivist did.

Nothing in this book asks to be believed. Belief is not the discipline here. The discipline is keeping: read what was kept, notice what is missing, and hold both without closing the gap. The book will not close it for you. That is the finding.

One sentence in this deposit is a working. You will know it when you reach it, because it is the first sentence of the estate and the last of this page, and because the estate’s whole doctrine is that it does not fail. It is printed here with the blank left blank. Notice what you are tempted to write in it.

ai_statement.title: The Hand and the Glass
ai_statement.subtitle: A statement on generative artificial intelligence
paragraphs: This book began in human inquiry: in engineering, history, archival practice, and the conversations between them. Its concepts, originating writings, and intellectual commitments are mine and those of my human collaborators, whose contributions retain their own attribution. They are intellectually sovereign from the tools used to develop and present them.

The Companion Dossier is the public body of work from which this novel grew. It has two doors: a website for exploring its writings, experiments, and conversations, and a GitHub repository, the online filing room holding the source documents, code, and record of changes. Begin with the website; turn to the repository to look behind it. Both addresses appear on the preceding page.

Generative AI served as a dialogic instrument in building that work. I supplied the writing, seeds, questions, and direction; Claude was the primary system through which I developed and assembled the repository. The dialogue helped me articulate, test, organize, and elaborate the material. The purposes of the inquiry and the judgment governing it remained human.

The summoned voices belong here as well. The exchanges gathered under From Beyond show the project using the method it studies: personae called into dialogue around a humanly supplied seed. These are AI-mediated voices, not testimony from the people whose names they bear. The instrument was used from within, and its traces were kept.

For the novel, I opened a Claude Code session with the entire repository, together with dozens of my handwritten notes and text files that constituted a rough outline of the book. A conservative estimate puts the repository’s readable text alone at more than three hundred printed pages. I worked through my conception in dialogue with Claude and used it to develop an initial draft from those materials and my direction. I read and revised that draft, then used later versions of Claude to workshop and strengthen the manuscript. Generated prose and editorial assistance belonged to a process I conceived, directed, and revised.

OpenAI tools assisted with editorial refinement, book design, typesetting, and production; OpenAI image tools were used for the cover artwork. The frontispiece and five record-opening plates are typeset presentations of material in this volume. The estate map was redrawn from the deposited plate.

Authorship here rests in intellectual responsibility and accountability. I attach my name, credentials, and standing to this edition and answer for its substance, including its errors and omissions. My collaborators retain credit for their contributions. The tools hold no authorial responsibility.

The novel asks what a voice can carry, and what the record can warrant. Its instruments are disclosed because the distinction matters within the work itself. The glass is shown. The hand remains answerable.
